content: Umbilical cord blood is a type of human blood that is collected from the placenta and umbilical cord after the umbilical cord has been detached from a newborn baby. This blood is a rich source of hematopoietic stem cells, which are used in transplantation procedures. Both public and private cord blood banks store cord blood. Public banks coordinate matching cord blood units to patients through the National Marrow Donor Program (NMDP), while private banks, which are for-profit organizations, store cord blood exclusively for the donor or their relatives. The medical community strongly supports public cord blood banking, but private banking is generally not recommended unless there is a family history of specific genetic diseases. In some countries, such as France and Italy, private cord blood banking is illegal and opposed by the European Group on Ethics in Science and New Technologies. Cord blood stem cells are more proliferative and have a higher likelihood of matching family members compared to stem cells from bone marrow. Parents and siblings share 50% of the genetic markers of the donor’s stem cells, but the probability of a successful match for transplantation is still relatively low due to the need for multiple genetic markers to align. Additional stem cells can be collected from the placenta through a process called Placenta Cord Banking. After the healthcare provider collects cord blood from the umbilical cord, the placenta is sent to a stem cell laboratory for further processing to extract additional stem cells. By banking both umbilical cord blood and placenta-derived stem cells, families can potentially double the number of CD34+ stem cells available for transplantation. The number of CD34+ cells in a transplant is a critical factor in achieving successful treatment outcomes and improving patient survival rates. Cord blood can be collected from the umbilical vein using two methods: before the placenta is delivered (in utero) or after the placenta is delivered (ex utero). In the ex utero method, cord blood is collected after the placenta is delivered and the umbilical cord is clamped off from the newborn. The placenta is placed in a sterile structure, and the blood is collected by gravity drainage, yielding 40–150 mL of cord blood. In the in utero method, cord blood is collected after the baby is delivered but before the placenta is delivered. Once collected, cord blood units must be immediately shipped to a cord blood bank for processing. At public cord blood banks, the blood is analyzed for infectious agents, tissue typing is performed, and red blood cells are removed before the cord blood is stored in liquid nitrogen for future use. New parents have the option to store their newborn’s cord blood at a private cord blood bank or donate it to a public cord blood bank. Private cord blood banking costs approximately $2,000 for collection and $125 per year for storage (as of 2007). Public cord blood donation is free for the donor, although some obstetricians may charge a collection fee. However, many obstetricians choose to donate their time for this process. Public donation is not universally available, but its accessibility is increasing, with several local cord blood banks in the United States now accepting donations from within their states. The first sibling-donor cord blood transplant was performed in 1988. Following this, the National Institutes of Health (NIH) awarded a grant to Dr. Pablo Rubinstein to establish the world’s first cord blood program at the New York Blood Center (NYBC) to create an inventory of non-embryonic stem cell units for unrelated, matched grafts. In 2005, University of Toronto researcher Peter Zandstra developed a method to increase the yield of cord blood stem cells, enabling their use in treating adults as well as children. When cryopreserved cord blood is needed, it is thawed, washed to remove the cryoprotectant, and injected into a patient’s vein. This type of treatment, where stem cells are collected from a donor, is called allogeneic treatment. When the cells are collected from the same patient who will use them, it is referred to as autologous treatment. If the cells are collected from identical individuals, it is called syngeneic treatment. Xenogeneic transfer, involving cells from different species, is still underdeveloped and has limited research potential. The medical community generally supports public cord blood banking, but private banking has raised ethical and practical concerns. The controversy revolves around differing assessments of the likelihood of successful use of stored cord blood. Estimates of the odds that a child will need an autologous stem cell transplant by age 20 vary widely, with proponents citing odds of 1:2,700, while the European Union Group on Ethics cites odds of 1:20,000. The group has questioned the legitimacy of commercial cord blood banks for autologous use, stating that they sell a service with no proven therapeutic value and raise serious ethical concerns. The World Marrow Donor Association has also stated that autologous cord blood cells are not recommended for treating childhood leukemia due to the presence of pre-leukemic cells at birth. Additionally, autologous cord blood carries the same genetic defects as the donor and should not be used to treat genetic diseases. Currently, there are no known protocols for using autologous cord blood stem cells in therapy. Since the late 1980s, cord blood stem cells have been used to treat various blood and immune-system-related genetic diseases, cancers, and disorders. Most treatments involve cells from unrelated donors due to medical issues with using one’s own cells. In 1993, Dr. Joanne Kurtzberg of Duke University Medical Center performed the first two successful unrelated donor cord blood transplants, one of which cured acute lymphoblastic leukemia. The principal diseases and disorders treated with cord blood are listed on the National Donor Marrow Program website. In 2005, U.S. Representative Chris Smith passed legislation to increase the use and research of cord blood stem cells. The bill, signed into law by President George W. Bush, authorized $265 million for stem cell therapy, umbilical cord blood, and bone marrow treatments. It also allocated $79 million for the collection of cord blood stem cells to expand the nation’s public cord blood supply by adding 150,000 new units to the inventory. The law aims to collect a genetically diverse cross-section of cord blood units to make matches available to 90% of patients in need. It also created a national registry to match cord blood for patients. The National Marrow Donor Program (NMDP) was selected to oversee these duties in 2006. The law also mandates that all cord blood deemed unsuitable for transplantation be donated for research purposes.
